# Envisioning a Humane and Accessible US Methadone Treatment System: Generating Policy and Practice Recommendations From the Liberate Methadone Movement

**Authors:** Noa Krawczyk; Jordan Scott; Megan Miller; Abby Coulter; Aaron Ferguson; David Frank; Ayana Jordan; Paul Joudrey; Simeon D. Kimmel; Ximena A. Levander; Ruth Potee; Kate E. Roberts; Danielle Russell; Rachel Simon; Kimberly L. Sue; Leslie W. Suen; Louise Vincent; Nicholas Voyles; Caty Simon

## Abstract

Methadone treatment (MT) for opioid use disorder saves lives, but the US MT system has long been dominated by punitive policies and practices that make MT inaccessible, burdensome, and traumatic for patients. After generations without changes to methadone regulations, a confluence of circumstance—including the COVID-19 pandemic and an overdose crisis that has taken over a million lives—has begun to shift the MT advocacy and political landscape. This commentary describes the building of the “Liberate Methadone” movement; a grassroots effort led by people with lived and living experience with methadone, addiction clinicians, researchers, community leaders, and people with many of these identities. The Liberate Methadone movement is dedicated to building a more accessible, equitable MT system that prioritizes patient health, promotes dignity, and is grounded in evidence. We describe the experience of planning and hosting a national conference and generating proceedings with recommendations for needed incremental and structural reforms within the US MT system. The lessons learned from this movement can motivate others across clinical, research, and policy roles to partner with and learn from patient and community-led groups, guiding needed reforms within systems of care. It is through these joint efforts and listening to those directly impacted groups who have been left out of the conversation for far too long, that we can successfully reduce overdose and suffering, toward better health, dignity, and thriving in our communities.

## Introduction: The Grave Need to Reform the US Methadone Treatment System

Expanding the use of methadone treatment (MT) for opioid use disorder (OUD) is a key strategy to address the US overdose crisis and ongoing public health emergency.1 Decades of successful use and hundreds of studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of MT in reducing risky opioid use and improving multiple health outcomes,1–3 including cutting overdose risk by half.4–6 In the current landscape where fentanyl dominates the illicit drug market, the importance of MT is greater than ever, as it is highly effective among people who use fentanyl.7,8

Despite MT’s effectiveness, it is vastly underutilized in the United States: In 2020, 311 531 people received MT, less than a tenth of the 7.6 million estimated to meet diagnostic criteria for OUD.4,9 Between 2010 and 2019, MT use rose a mere 39% in the United States, relative to a 222% rise in buprenorphine use.4 Both treatments are considered gold-standard medications for OUD, with methadone leading to higher treatment retention than buprenorphine.10 However, buprenorphine can be prescribed in office-based settings and dispensed in pharmacies, while methadone for OUD can only be accessed via highly structured opioid treatment programs (OTPs).

Extensive regulation of OTPs by the federal Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), and state and local laws, have made it difficult to establish new OTPs.11–13 As a result, nearly 2500 (80% of) counties, home to 24% of the US population, do not have OTPs.14 MT is therefore nearly impossible to access for many patients who need it, particularly for those who live in rural areas, have mobility limitations, are institutionalized (e.g., incarcerated15 or living in nursing homes), or otherwise have to travel long distances to access the nearest clinic.16,17 Such scarce MT availability also increases risk for potentially deadly service disruptions in natural disaster settings such as hurricanes or fires, or infectious disease (COVID-19) outbreaks.18

Even patients who can physically reach OTPs routinely experience life-disrupting and often dehumanizing requirements as a condition of receiving care. Regulations that govern OTPs and the related treatment culture that has emerged from them are highly punitive and far from patient-centered. MT patients typically have little say in their own care, and are often forced to visit OTP clinics on a daily basis to take medication under the direct observation of clinic staff. In many cases, dosing decisions are made based on OTP rules rather than individualized treatment decisions or needs. Patients are additionally bound to multiple requirements to receive care, including mandatory counseling, observed urine drug testing, and strict expectations of abstinence from any drug.19 These requirements are not based on existing evidence of best clinical practices but rather on decades of status quo culture and norms within MT programs. All these requirements make MT extremely burdensome, especially for patients with disabilities, those who lack transportation, or have competing work and childcare responsibilities.17,20 Decades of research document traumatic patient experiences in the OTP system, which has been described by many as embodying a system of social control21–23 and “culture of cruelty.”20,24 Such barriers place additional stress on patients and can exacerbate risky drug use, as many are forced to the highly volatile illicit market or diverted methadone.25

The punitive OTP system is inextricably linked to the US Drug War—a political campaign long since discredited and known to be detrimental to people who use drugs, especially those from poor and racially marginalized communities.26–29 Drug War rhetoric prioritized control of poor and racial/ethnic minoritized communities over the promotion of health.26,30–32 As OTPs were historically designed for and are still concentrated in racially minoritized communities,33 patients from marginalized groups often bear the greatest burden of this system, exacerbating racial disparities and stigma.30 Indeed, recent decades have seen some evidence of worse treatment access and mixed retention outcomes among minoritized racial/ethnic groups,34–36 possibly contributing to rising disparities in overdose deaths across the country.37,38

The current MT system is a detriment to existing patients and deters others from initiating treatment. Further complicating this landscape is that the majority of OTPs are for-profit organizations, and nearly one-third are operated by 3 private equity firms.39 Commercial interests often conflict with patient needs and efforts to change practices.39,40 Some provider and patient groups have been calling for changes to regulations and OTP culture for generations, but have been largely ignored. For example, as far back as the 1970s, the Methadone Association for Social and Economic Equality and the Methadone Coalition for Equal Opportunity worked to advocate for the rights of methadone patients.41,42 Despite a largely ineffective and seemingly intractable MT system in the United States, alternative systems of methadone delivery have been operating for decades in some other countries, proving to be both safe and effective: Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom, and France,43,44 for example, use a combination of physician prescribing, pharmacy dispensing, and specialty clinics to provide MT for OUD patients.45 US feasibility studies of pharmacy-dispensed MT for OUD also find this model to be effective and welcomed by patients.46,47 Moreover, simulation studies show that expanding MT from the ~2000 OTPs to the ~70 000 existing US community pharmacies could transform access to MT and significantly alleviate burden, cost, and stigma.16,48 Such a shift to office-based methadone had been proposed in the US Federal Register in 1999, but never passed.49 In sum, the need to advocate, plan for, and implement an alternative US MT system that is accessible, humane, and person-centered is long overdue.

### Seizing the Moment: COVID-19 and the Opportunity for Change

After decades of stasis, a number of circumstances began to shift the MT advocacy and political landscape.50,51 Worsening overdose deaths over the past decade, along with unprecedented MT regulatory changes introduced during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, instigated a wave of advocacy, research, and political interest in reforming US MT structures.52,53 The COVID-19 regulatory changes that would later become permanent in 2024, allowed, for the first time, greater flexibility around take-home doses, where new patients could receive up to 14 or 28 days of take-home doses if considered stable. This was a vast change from the prior rules that prevented patients from receiving any take-homes for at least 3 months, but often required daily visits for months or even years.54,55 A plethora of scientific studies found that pandemic-era regulatory changes allowing for increased flexibility for methadone take-home doses from OTPs were both safe and highly desirable by patients.56–60 At the same time, the slow uptake of these flexibilities by OTPs highlighted the MT system’s deeply ingrained resistance to change, stemming from a decades-long culture of punitive practices, powerful commercial interests, and a patronizing treatment structure upheld by methadone regulations and program requirements.26,61–63

These changes sparked a revitalization of advocacy efforts spearheaded by people with lived and living experience (PWLLE) with methadone, demanding permanent changes to MT and a greater voice for patients at the table. In 2020, the US national drug users union, National Survivors Union (then called Urban Survivors Union), disseminated a sign-on letter citing a list of patient demands and calling for broad organizational support.64–66 The letter was signed by over 140 organizations, including the International Certification & Reciprocity Consortium, a governing body that accredits counseling staff at OTPs and former Drug Czar Michael Botticelli. National Survivors Union then published 2 versions of a document entitled the “Methadone Manifesto”: One white paper and one peer-reviewed article published in the American Journal of Public Health, which summarized grievances of people in MT within the current OTP system and outlined a path forward for better care.24,67 Inspired by these grassroots efforts and directly called to join advocacy efforts by PWLLE, allies, including addiction clinicians, researchers, and community advocates in support of MT reform, joined with drug user-led groups to form the National Coalition to Liberate Methadone (NCLM).68 This group’s primary goal is to focus on what has never been done in previous MT advocacy efforts: Bring together diverse voices to advocate for a more humane and accessible MT system that prioritizes patient health, promotes dignity, and is grounded in evidence. NCLM was established with the mission of inclusion, aiming to build relationships with reciprocity between traditional research and medical institutions and PWLLE. PWLLE in NCLM are community and academic researchers, providers, workforce managers, and nationally and internationally acclaimed movement thought leaders. NCLM acknowledges intersecting and multidimensional roles and experiences and welcomes sometimes uncomfortable discussions among diverse members on how best to reform MT.

The changing MT landscape also sparked attention from leading government, medical, and scientific institutions: In 2022, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine hosted an event on methadone that included discussions about the COVID-19 reforms, and included NCLM members as speakers and event planners.69 Here, even DEA and SAMHSA representatives agreed that expanding MT and addressing disparities in access were key federal priorities.70 Around the same time, NIH National Institute of Drug Abuse (NIDA) Director Nora Volkow directly called for the expansion of MT reforms,71 and a prominent NIDA Clinical Trials Network Task Force published an agenda for priority research areas to expand the use of MT.72 President Biden’s 2022 Drug Control Strategy even explicitly recommended regulators consider methadone pharmacy dispensing.73 This shift in conversation opened up a platform and the traction needed to build a vision for a more equitable and effective MT system.

### The Liberating Methadone Conference: A National Gathering Centering Voices of Those With Lived and Living Experience

Building on this momentum, in September 2023, the NCLM—in partnership with National Survivors Union, Medication Assisted Treatment Support & Awareness, and other MT advocates and academic partners—organized a 2-day hybrid conference to discuss and exchange ideas on how to improve access to and use of MT. Over 800 people registered for the conference—half in-person and half remotely—with representation across 44 US states and 10 countries. The conference, named “Liberating Methadone: Building A Community and Roadmap for Change,” aimed to break down traditional silos between researchers, clinicians, policymakers, and PWLLE. The gathering created a shared space to integrate scientific, clinical, and lived experience expertise to build a roadmap to transform the MT system. At its core was the vision to build an accessible, effective, and equitable MT system, rooted in the experiences and needs of individuals receiving MT.

Multiple government, foundation, and institutional funds supported conference activities and scholarships, which were brought in through a combination of grant applications and outreach to foundations by conference organizers. Importantly, these funds supported free registration for all participants, in addition to 31 travel awards provided to PWLLE to attend the conference from all over the country. Organizers made arrangements with a local OTP to provide guest methadone dosing for participants in MT. A virtual option for the conference was provided for those unable to travel to the conference due to physical, health, time, or financial constraints. All these elements were critical to ensuring attendance of PWLLE, facilitating an inclusive space that centered the voices of people most directly impacted by the MT system.

The two-day gathering consisted of a range of activities deliberating current challenges and limitations of MT practice, policy, and research, and discussing future directions to inform a better system of care. Activities included panel discussions, skill-building workshops, and a poster session highlighting research presentations and reports from the community and PWLLE (whose abstracts were recently published in a proceedings supplement).74 Facilitated break-out groups were organized to gather participant recommendations, and a direct-action event was held where participants could publicly call for reforms to end the Drug War and honor loved ones who had been lost to overdose. PWLLE were both organizers and participants of every session, along with addiction clinicians, treatment providers, researchers, state and federal policymakers overseeing substance use treatment services, and even a member of Congress who attended the conference.

### Proceedings and Recommendations: Six Focus Areas to Guide a National Agenda for MT Reform

Critical to the goal of the Liberating Methadone conference was ensuring the ideas and priorities generated throughout this event would live on to inform the agenda for advocacy efforts going forward. To do this, conference organizers gathered detailed notes and materials from each session. Then, 2 working groups were convened to synthesize content generated into actionable recommendations, with 1 group focusing on clinical practice recommendations and the second on policy recommendations. Working group participants were carefully selected based on MT expertise. Deliberate efforts were made to acknowledge multi-positionality among participants who wear many hats and have intersecting experiences, including lived and living experience as well as clinical, research, and policy expertise delivering, studying or overseeing MT. Professional facilitators were brought in to help direct discussions, conciliate disagreements, refine and gather consensus on recommendations, and draft the initial report. The report with final recommendations was reviewed and iteratively revised by the organizing committee and all working group members, along with a few external reviewers working in MT research and policy.

The final proceedings report was published in June of 2024 and was disseminated widely to drug user activist groups and networks of PWLLE, as well as MT research, policy, and practice audiences.75 The following 6 recommendations were identified as focus areas toward a more humane and accessible system of MT, and each contain specific examples and specifications for how these reforms can be implemented:

- Center living and lived experience in policy and practice: Placing PWLLE in decision-making roles; diversifying the methadone practice and research workforce; and ensuring policies, practices, and research are informed by and responsive to the needs of people in MT.

- Normalize MT as standard healthcare: Establishing novel MT training and educational infrastructure, shifting stigmatizing perceptions of MT, and improving standards of practice to promote MT as a legitimate and necessary medical service across multiple healthcare settings.

- Ground MT in person-centeredness: Centering the individual goals and safety of MT patients by framing treatment around patient-defined goals, prioritizing trust and connection to care over punitive measures, and generating data on person-centered outcomes.

- Improve OTP practices: Shifting the culture of OTPs towards person-centered care, reducing barriers to and burdensome requirements of OTPs, enhancing comprehensive care services within OTPs, and increasing transparency and patient protections.

- Create alternatives to the current opioid treatment system: Expanding methadone distribution to non-OTPs via office-based settings, allowing physicians and advanced practice providers to prescribe and pharmacists to dispense methadone for OUD, and supporting MT coordination across various healthcare settings.

- Shift public thinking about MT: Amplifying MT success stories, raising awareness of MT’s value, and reducing stigma, particularly among communities disproportionately impacted by the overdose crisis and the Drug War.

Each focus area included detailed recommendations on specific actions that should be taken by different target groups, including federal and state governments, MT providers and programs, clinicians and their licensing bodies, researchers, community leaders, and other key groups to achieve these overarching goals (see select examples in Table 1, and full report for details).75

### Lessons Learned and Next Steps: The Power of Coalition Building to Improve Substance Use Health Services and Practices

The Liberate Methadone movement illustrates the power that can be generated from gathering multiple uniquely positioned groups to advocate for change, even in a system that has felt frustratingly intractable for decades. The movement synthesizes the voices of multiple key and intersecting groups that each bring their own forms of knowledge, power, and social capital. At the forefront of NCLM are PWLLE, who not only bring their personal life experience but are experts and leaders in patient and clinic advocacy and reform, as well as policy advocacy grassroots mobilization. PWLLE maintain long-term relationships with policy makers, institutions, and community groups. Addiction clinicians bring clinical expertise, deep familiarity with healthcare systems and how to change them, and their positions of power as trusted messengers. Researchers add access to networks and resources through academic institutions as well as expertise in leveraging research to drive evidence-based social and policy advocacy. Finally, policy partners and champions bring deep familiarity with the landscape and intricacies of the policy-making process at multiple levels of government. These groups are far from mutually exclusive, as most members hold positions that intersect across lived and living experience, research, practice, policy, and advocacy. By maintaining a strong dedication to centering PWLLE as the leading voice in key decisions, the reforms proposed reflect the genuine needs of the MT patient population. Moreover, this approach serves to build trust, credibility, and capacity among those who have been stigmatized, maltreated, and marginalized from mainstream substance use treatment and policy discussions. The lessons learned from this movement can motivate others across clinical, research, and policy roles to partner with and learn from patient and community-led groups to guide important reforms within systems of care.

The work of the Liberate Methadone movement is just the beginning of what will require a dedicated and long-term approach to continue moving the proposed recommendations forward. The highly problematic culture of the US MT system—which has deep-seated commercial conflicts and has been built on generations of structural racism, marginalization, and scapegoating of people who use drugs—will not be undone overnight. Still, the Liberate Methadone community and movement have been firmly established, with the group continuing to iterate and advocate for the necessary changes that will improve access to and quality of this life-saving treatment. Since the conference, and in part as a result of advocacy efforts by the Liberate Methadone movement, there have been important changes in MT policy: In 2024, SAMHSA released a revised rule, making COVID-19 flexibilities for methadone take-homes and other long-awaited changes permanent, a small yet significant step towards making MT more patient-centered.76 The impact of these new policies will depend on the political will of federal, state, and OTP leaders to implement these changes, and continued advocacy efforts will be needed to ensure uptake of novel flexibilities in practice. Still, this new law signals critical acknowledgment by federal leaders of the need to update and revise outdated MT policies and practices. Additionally, for the first time in history, a bill was introduced in Congress to expand MT to physician-prescribing and dispensing from pharmacies—the Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act.77 The next years will determine whether elected officials will choose to endorse changes that would further align our system with that of other developed countries and substantially transform the MT delivery landscape to improve access and quality of care.63,78 If, on the other hand, our leaders defy calls for reform, we risk continued marginalization of our most effective treatment for OUD, and maintaining an ineffective system that will not be prepared to meet and adapt to future substance use epidemics.

Achieving the vision of a humane and accessible MT system both in the United States and globally will require prioritizing the voices of PWLLE. It will necessitate courage from politicians, healthcare system leaders, substance use treatment providers and teams, and our broader communities to demand both incremental and structural reforms to MT policies and practices. Even if policy reforms are achieved, a continued movement of advocates with lived and living experience and expertise across medicine, policy, and healthcare delivery will be needed to ensure thoughtful implementation that maximizes access to safe and dignified treatment for OUD. It is through these joint efforts, building bridges and conversations with reciprocity across diverse groups, and listening to those most directly affected, that we will successfully reduce overdose and suffering, toward better health, dignity, and thriving in our communities.
